item.title: I replaced Google Photos with Immich on a Raspberry Pi, and my phone backs up to it automatically
item.itunes:title: I replaced Google Photos with Immich on a Raspberry Pi, and my phone backs up to it automatically
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve spent a lot of time tinkering with Docker containers, LXCs, and Podman environments, and most of these projects revolved around self-hosting my own services. And considering that containerized services typically don’t need a lot of computational horsepower, even the weakest devices in my arsenal can hold their own against self-hosted tools.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Data archival platforms, for example, mesh well with outdated systems, and Immich is a great example of this notion. In fact, I recently tried deploying it on an old Raspberry Pi 5 module, and this single-board computer could easily drive most of its image archival tools once I armed it with some extra storage provisions.

I self-hosted a Google Photos alternative with a Synology NAS — here's how it went

Build your own photo management platform with a NAS!

11
By  Rich Edmonds

Immich is more cost-effective than Google Photos in the long run

And that’s before you consider its privacy perks

If you’ve only got a few gigabytes of photos you wish to preserve, the pricing tiers on Google Photos (or rather, Google One) don’t seem too bad. The free plan can accommodate up to 15GB of media, while the $1.99/month basic plan lets you go up to 100GB, and you can pay around $2 more every month to upgrade to 200GB.

Unfortunately, the problem begins when you’ve got images and videos that hog hundreds of GBs. Google’s AI Plus subscription, for example, requires you to shell out $4.99/month for 400GB of storage space. My photo collection alone consumes more GBs than that plan, and if I were to include all the images I’d like to back up for my family, I’d have to shell out $9.99 every month (or $99.99 when billed annually) for the 2TB plan.

This sum gets pretty high when I run the numbers for a few years. Meanwhile, a self-hosted Immich instance could run on a Raspberry Pi 5 that I already own. A 2TB HDD costs around $120, and this upfront investment is fairly cheap considering that I’d otherwise have to pay around a hundred bucks on Google One’s 2TB plan, anyway.

Then there’s the privacy aspect that often gets overlooked when it comes to cloud platforms. Sure, storing images on Google’s servers is fairly simple, and with the right plan, you also get to tinker with different AI tools. But personally, I’d rather keep my private family photos far away from the cloud, especially since I’ve already created a generative AI-powered pipeline for editing my images on Krita.

With enough storage, even a Raspberry Pi 5 can handle Immich

I’ve offloaded the machine-learning tasks to my daily driver

Although a simple Immich server doesn’t require a lot of firepower, I wanted to keep resource consumption to a bare-minimum. So, I went with a simple DietPi instance as the underlying OS, with a rootless Docker setup acting as the container runtime. For now, I’ve connected an external 2TB HDD to my Raspberry Pi 5, as I’ve yet to buy a dedicated SATA HAT for my tiny tinkering companion. But since I’m already supplying enough power to the SBC, a single external HDD shouldn’t be a problem.

Just like typical Docker containers, deploying Immich was a cakewalk. First, I pulled Immich’s docker-compose.yml and example.env files from the official docs. Then, I edited the latter to use my USB-powered HDD for the library and renamed it to .env. Once I’d run the docker compose up -d command, Docker began working its containerization magic, and my Immich server went online within a few minutes.

UI-wise, Immich has a similar design as Google Photos, and it borrows plenty of archival, sorting, and image sharing features from its cloud rival. Just to test things out, I uploaded around a hundred review images to Immich, and the upload process was wrapped up in a few seconds. Just like Google Photos, Immich supports albums and memories-esque photo collections, and I was able to configure extra user accounts for my family.

Besides letting the other denizens of my household store their images, Immich also lets me share individual albums with my family, and the Cast functionality works just as well when I want to display my media on a projector, TV, or another device. Although I don’t use it very often, Immich supports reverse-geocoding and map view, which make sorting images a lot easier.

To my surprise, my Raspberry Pi 5 was able to perform OCR analysis pretty well. However, Immich supports other AI-powered services that require a bit more processing oomph, which is where my daily driver comes into the equation. Immich lets me configure a remote processing system for machine-learning tasks, and I was able to deploy this service as a Docker container on my PC.

That way, my Raspberry Pi Immich hub can remain online 24/7 and trigger the smart search, facial recognition, and duplicate detection pipelines when my PC comes online. And I haven’t even mentioned Immich’s best perk yet …

Immich’s robust mobile app is the real star of the show

Thanks to Tailscale, I can back up photos outside my home network

Google Photos’ ability to create automatic backups of everything you capture on your phone is pretty neat, and Immich manages to replicate this feature to a T. Typical self-hosted services don’t have mobile apps at all, and the ones that do often have half-baked instances that leave a lot to be desired.

Immich, on the other hand, has a mobile app that can not only provide a smartphone-sized UI for accessing my photo collection, but also copy photos and videos automatically to my Raspberry Pi server. Heck, the app even includes provisions for clearing my smartphones’ storage after a specific date, so my backed up media don’t hog too much space on my portable companion.

I’ve also got Tailscale running on a separate Raspberry Pi Zero board, and thanks to its subnet router functionality, my smartphone can access the Immich server even when I’m away from my tinkering cave.

But even with all these perks, I can’t quite call my Immich instance a backup server as is, because my photos can become irretrievable if something were to happen to it. And between random HDD failure, fire, theft, and other untoward incidents, there are plenty of risks in storing everything on a single server – which is where Google Photos gets the upper hand.

However, I’ve already got an old NAS set up at a relative’s place, and since it’s already on my tailnet, I use it as a secondary backup node. For my Docker-based Immich container, I’ve deployed a Kopia instance to sync its library and database with my remote server every week. That way, I’d still be able to recover my precious media even if my Raspberry Pi hub became unusable.

I stopped paying for 3 cloud subscriptions after deploying Immich, Vaultwarden, and Nextcloud on a mini PC

The mini PC paid for itself in months.

5
By  Jasmine Mannan

Build a cheap image management server with Immich

Personally, the only reason I chose a Raspberry Pi for this project is that I had one lying around after buying a bunch of them in 2023. But considering its current prices, I wouldn’t recommend grabbing the board in this day and age. That’s because Immich runs well on most devices, including old laptops and outdated gaming machines, and you don’t need to spend money on expensive hardware just to build a Google Photos replacement.

But if you’re more interested in the backup and recovery aspect of Google’s cloud platform, I’d recommend picking up any ol’ x86 system for your Immich hub. Refurbished mini-PCs can cost under $100, and you can arm them with a cheap HDD or two for your Kopia/Borg backup tasks.

Even with the electricity costs of running a remote server every few days, this 3-2-1 backup setup would still cost less than the more expensive plans on Google One. And the fact that everything remains on your own hardware is just the icing on top.

item.title: I asked Claude Code to build a racer with splitscreen and DualSense support, and it delivered a Steam-ready game
item.itunes:title: I asked Claude Code to build a racer with splitscreen and DualSense support, and it delivered a Steam-ready game
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Last week, I put three coding agents against each other with the same prompt to build a game, and Claude Code, running Sonnet 5.5, ended up surprising me with a breathtaking 3D racer with DualSense support that beat nearly every single game that I've seen it code. I was quick to share the game with a few of my colleagues, who, like myself, believed that a game this well-built was sitting on a gold mine of potential.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

One idea kept coming back to me all this while. Split-screen used to be a staple of racing games back in the day, and now, I rarely see it in new releases. So I went back to the same project and asked Claude Code to take its own codebase a little further. One prompt and about 14 minutes later, it delivered the game that I'd asked for in a single HTML file, and it had made decisions that I never even thought to ask for.

Claude Code's racer had everything, except a second player

Racing your own ghost only goes so far

Ghostline, as Claude itself named it, is a 3D time-trial racer that runs straight from a folder on my PC. While writing the prompt to create it, I was going for the simplicity that was characteristic of a .io game that you could just jump into with nothing to install, no need to commit, and pure arcade racing from the second you launch. The game's three tracks take you from a sunset coastline to an alpine climb and a neon city at night.

It's almost fascinating how feature-packed the game is, considering that it is fewer than 3,200 lines of code. It works with a DualSense controller right out of the box, lowers its own render resolution if the frame rate dips, and gives the curbs and grass their own grip levels, so cutting corners costs you time.

For all of that, though, it was still just a little project that you'd open every once in a while to appreciate how far AI-assisted coding had come. For it to be a game that I could enjoy with my friends, it needed to have something that my five-year-old self would have expected from any racing game, and that was a split-screen mode.

I used Claude Code, Google Antigravity and OpenAI Codex to develop an app, and found only one worth using

Vibe coding is here to stay, and it has only one champion

33
By  Abhinav Raj

Claude Code added split-screen without breaking single-player

It was easier than waiting for a DLC

With my prompt, I deliberately kept things simple and didn't specify the technical aspects of how a split-screen mode should work in execution. I simply asked for a two-player mode that left the existing game's time trial mode, best laps, and ghosts as they were.

Each player could join with their own DualSense controller, the screen would split top and bottom with its HUD for each half, and the race would run three laps with the ghost switched off. I also asked for cars to be able to bump into each other, for vibration to reach only the right controller, and for a results screen at the end of the race with an option to rematch.

Sonnet 5.5 wrapped the entire thing in about 14 minutes, which was less than half the time it took it to build the original from scratch. It put the whole mode in a single new file and gave the existing ones small hooks that leave single-player as it was. Since it had built its own renderer the first time around, teaching it to draw onto half the screen only took a handful of lines: 

region(x, y, w, h) {
this.aspect = w / h;
this.gl.viewport(x, y, w, h);
}

At this point, it seemed like a simple and straightforward job, at least that's what I thought. However, it then did something that grabbed my interest. Sonnet 5.5 took the call to run the old and the new code side by side on identical inputs, and noted that the physics matched exactly over 153,234 steps. Only then did it proceed to test the two simulated DualSense controllers through joining, pausing, full races, and even accounting for controller disconnects.

Someone got Claude to play GTA 4 just ahead of GTA 6's release

We got Claude Code playing GTA 4 before GTA 6.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

The two-player mode is full of improvisations I never asked for

If you win the race, you can't get in the way anymore

The game itself is a dream from a user experience point of view, and that was something that I noticed from the very first launch. Each player gets to join the race by pressing X on their DualSense, which plays a chime to confirm, and the race starts from a side-by-side grid with the screen split top and bottom. Cars bump and release yellow sparks when they touch, and Claude Code treats each one as a capsule the length of the car.

Upon inspecting the code itself, I noticed that every knock could scrub off between 2% to 8% of your speed depending on how hard you hit. That was a level of meticulousness that I genuinely did not anticipate going in. 

if (closing < 0.5 || state.cool > 0) return null;
const keep = 1 - U.clamp(0.02 + 0.003 * closing, 0.02, 0.08);
a.vx *= keep; a.vz *= keep; b.vx *= keep; b.vz *= keep;
state.cool = BUMP.cooldown;

My favorite touch, by far, however, is what happens after you cross the finish line, and that's something that I discovered by accident, owing to the fact that my partner was an entire lap behind me during our race. Once a car crosses the finish line, it stops being solid, so a player that's still racing drives straight through the winner instead of crashing into a parked car: 

// A car that has taken the flag is out of the way: no contact with it.
if (a.started && !a.finished && !b.finished) {

As for the rest of the mode, it feels just as considered. The results screen ignores input for nearly a second so nobody can skip it by mashing buttons on the controller, and fascinatingly enough, every rematch swaps grid sides. Customization is also possible by changing the car's colors, which helps to not get confused in the middle of the race as both cars are based on the same model. To be fair though, that was something that the original had as well.

All it took was a prompt, and a second controller

Perhaps the true magic of the game is just the amalgamation of how all of these invisible little fine touches make for an enjoyable experience. The game itself transported me back to the days of when I used to play split-screen racers in the PS2 era, and that is not a feeling that I expected that a prompt would be able to bring back.

// A car that has taken the flag is out of the way: no contact with it.
if (a.started && !a.finished && !b.finished) {

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have old devices lying around, and so probably do you. In fact, before I started this project I didn’t realize how many old devices were hidden in drawers around my house. But as soon as I saw the PrivateLM project, I knew I had to dig up all the discarded, old phones and tablets (some with broken screens) I could find. Why? Because this project promised to turn them into a cluster that could run LLMs these phones individually had no business running.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Not only that, but the cluster could sit on my WiFi network and serve those LLMs using OpenAI’s APIs to any harness I wanted to point at it. Let the jaw dropping commence.

From trash to treasure

A desperate scramble to dig up old devices

Suddenly, all those old devices we had somewhere, had become important again. I scrounged up everything I could find: my daughter’s old Nokia whose USB-C port struggled to connect well enough to charge, my wife’s Samsung Galaxy Tab S6 Lite with a cracked (but functional) screen, my no-name, generic Android tablet I bought off Amazon for $100 (something called an "Antemper"), and more. I even enlisted the help of my Boox Go Color 7 e-reader (which runs Android).

Here’s what made up my cluster:

  • A Moto G 2025.
  • A Nokia TA-1085.

item.title: This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me
item.itunes:title: This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you do any type of creative work, you’ve probably had at least one Adobe subscription, or thought about getting one. I used to shuffle through pretty much every Adobe plan – All Apps, Photography, and the individual apps. Most people end up in this predicament because we usually need at least one app for images, another for videos, and so on. I ended up canceling all my subscriptions this year because of this subscription fatigue.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I’ve migrated my entire workflow to free and open-source apps now, and continue to discover new options every week. There’s one open-source tool I’ve overlooked, however – Blender. This 3D modeling app has never been the first to come to mind for my graphics and video editing stack, but I underestimated its capabilities. Turns out, not only can you create 3D models with it, but you can also edit images, videos, and do motion graphics. After giving it a proper spin, I realized it could replace Photoshop, Premiere, and After Effects.

What is Blender?

It’s more than a 3D modeling app

Blender is a free, open-source 3D modeling app first and foremost, but it expands into much more than that. It covers the entire 3D creation process, from modeling and rigging to animation and rendering. Artists use Blender to create everything from animated films and visual graphics to 3D models and virtual reality environments. A lot of major films have used Blender for some of their graphics, including Captain America: The Winter Soldier.

So you might wonder, how does Blender, a 3D modeling tool, compete with Adobe’s ecosystem, which mainly consists of image and video editing tools? Well, Blender has various workspaces, including options for video editing, image editing, and motion graphics. This makes it an all-in-one powerhouse that can effectively replace pretty much all of your Adobe subscriptions. Here’s how…

Using Blender as an image editor

Replacing Photoshop

Blender was the last tool I ever thought I’d use as a Photoshop alternative. But it has a workspace called Compositing, which functions as an image editor. Some people use the UV Editing workspace for images, but it’s not non-destructive like Compositing. Right out of the gate, you’ll notice the setup is completely different from Photoshop; that’s because it’s node-based rather than layer-based.

Node editing takes some getting used to, but the upside is that you get precise, non-destructive adjustments. Each effect creates its own node, and you can stack them however you like between the image and the output view. Blender has loads of options here, from color correction and color grading tools to chroma keying and masking for subject isolation; there’s even a render window with some brush options. It also supports a wide range of color spaces, alpha channels, and even Z Depth, if you know how to set it up. It’s pretty much everything you’d find in Photoshop and then some, just in a completely different layout.

Using Blender’s video editor

Replacing Premiere Pro

Blender has always had a dedicated video editing workspace called VSE (video sequence editor). I’ve used it for a couple of video projects before, and it’s surprisingly normal. It’s a multi-layer editor with a standard layout that has your media on the top-left, timeline at the bottom, viewer in the middle, and effects on the right. It has all your basics, such as splitting and trimming, plus some animation options like transitions and transform controls.

Furthermore, you can edit the lighting and colors, add effects, add text, and create masks for things like background removal. All of this is tied together nicely with Blender’s keyframe abilities, which is how you’ll animate all the adjustments and effects. Not only does Blender’s VSE replace Premiere Pro, but it also integrates with the other workspaces. This means I can switch to a different workspace and enable 3D rendering for my video.

Animating graphics in Blender

Replacing After Effects

Blender’s Geometry Nodes window is what makes it a real After Effects alternative. It’s a procedural system that lets you create, modify, and animate objects through connected nodes. So, once again, I’m working with a node-based editor here as opposed to layers, meaning I’ve got precise control over my elements and effects. You can do 3D objects in this space, but I prefer sticking to the flat geometry.

The library is packed with effects like patterns, colors, and textures, and you can animate all of it using the transform controls and keyframes. This setup allows for parameter-based animations, meaning I can control all my elements with a few sliders. You can render the final creation and export it as a video, and you can also mix Geometry Nodes with the Compositor for more layered effects. This has been the perfect space to create animated overlays and backgrounds for my video projects – but you can create anything from particle effects to abstract and generative designs.

The all-in-one tool that replaces Adobe’s creative suite

I didn’t expect a 3D modeling tool to be a broad-spectrum Adobe replacement, but it genuinely replaces all three of these tools. There is a learning curve, especially if you’re used to layer-based editing, but once you get used to nodes, you actually have a little more control than in Adobe software. It’s an entire ecosystem of image, video, and motion editors rolled into one app.

Blender

item.title: My old Android phone now runs my whole retro gaming library on the TV, and it works great with a controller
item.itunes:title: My old Android phone now runs my whole retro gaming library on the TV, and it works great with a controller
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
These days, retro gaming has become incredibly easy. You don't need a powerful PC to emulate some of the most iconic consoles of all time, so even an old laptop, mini PC, Raspberry Pi, or even a phone can be used to play your favorite games. Of course, you may not always have the optimal device for your preferred playing experience, but in reality, the ideal setup may be lying dormant in your house.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

To prove it, I decided to take my old Android phone and turn it into a retro gaming console that lives on my TV. All it takes is RetroArch, ES-DE, and a couple of accessories to make it all work.

What I needed

A couple of accessories and apps

Of course, if you're going to turn your phone into the centerpiece for your living room gaming setup, you need a couple of things. First off, a Bluetooth controller. I had my Xbox Wireless Controller lying around already, and it's a great option, but you can also find much cheaper models on Amazon depending on your needs. A great maker of Bluetooth controllers is 8BitDo, so I recommend looking through that catalog to see if something suits your preferences.

To connect my phone to a TV, I also needed a USB hub or dock. You could find a USB-C to HDMI adapter, but you also need to keep your phone charged if you want it to stay plugged into the TV, so one of these hubs gives you the option to connect a charger as well as an HDMI port. You can find USB-C hubs from companies like Anker and Ugreen in the $20 range that include both USB-C power delivery and HDMI ports, so it's not a huge investment. I'm using a much more expensive model, but only because it's the only one I currently have at home.

Otherwise, you'll want to make your phone more friendly to use said controller, and emulation frontends are the best way to go about it. RetroArch is a solid enough option on its own, but ES-DE is one of the best frontends out there, and it also exists for Android. However, the Android version of ES-DE does require you to pay up, and it's not on the Play Store. You can get it directly from the team's Patreon, or buy on the Samsung Galaxy Store or Huawei AppGallery (if you're in a market where Huawei sells its phones).

I finally organized my emulator collection, and this free frontend made it feel better than a real console

It makes everything feel natural

2
By  João Carrasqueira

If you're not willing to pay up, you can always stick with RetroArch to handle it all. It's still a solid experience overall. Though, keep in mind, the Play Store version of RetroArch is noticeably out of date and not maintained anymore. You'll need to get it from the official website.

One thing to note is that some phones may not support display output over USB-C. That shouldn't be a problem for most devices, but if you can, give it a shot before investing too much time and money into the project.

Setting up is easy

Frontends save you a lot of time

With everything installed, you then have to set things up to make it relatively seamless. I had already configured RetroArch for a previous project, and I recommend starting with it to save yourself headaches later. RetroArch lets you download various emulators as "cores" so it's easy to manage them all in one place. You just have to go into the app and download the cores for the platforms you plan to emulate.

In my case, that includes Game Boy, Game Boy Color, NES, SNES, Nintendo 64, and even GameCube, though which platforms are viable will depend on how powerful your old phone is. For some phones, something like the GameCube may be pushing it. This is a phone with a Snapdragon 865 chipset, so it's on the higher end of the spectrum.

You can choose the emulators you prefer for each platform. You may also want to tweak the controls for RetroArch, specifically the button configuration to open the quick menu in games. This is crucial if you want to exit a game back into ES-DE later, and it's something that always gives me headaches when I forget to configure it.

Setting up ES-DE is much easier. Simply launch the app and it will guide you through selecting where to store its own app data, as well as selecting your ROM folder. It may be easier to move ROMs over to your phone beforehand and pointing ES-DE to it, but you can do it the other way around if you prefer. Then, it's just a couple of taps until you're in ES-DE proper. By default, the UI shows on-screen controls, but since I'm using a controller, I disabled this in the app's settings.

Otherwise, this just works. ES-DE loads a beautiful, simplistic UI (you can always install extra themes if you want to change it up), showing me all my consoles and I can then choose games from there. I can also use scraping services to fetch metadata for my games and make the presentation even better.

It's a great retro console

But GameCube is a bit much

With all of this set up, I was able to start using my phone as a gaming console, and it has some notable perks over something like a mini PC. Phones are low-power devices and the Arm architecture is very efficient, so this setup can run just fine without a single fan causing unwanted noise.

Despite that, performance is pretty solid. All of the platforms I mentioned run well, except GameCube games don't perform at the best of their abilities. I tried playing The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess and Super Mario Sunshine, and it definitely felt a bit stuttery in some cases, especially when water was involved, but it was playable.

I turned my old Google TV box into the easiest way to play retro games on my TV

Why add another box to your living room?

By  João Carrasqueira

Otherwise, everything runs great here, all the way up to Nintendo 64 titles. I played games like Super Mario Bros. on the NES, Super Metroid on the SNES, Toki Tori on the Game Boy Color, and Banjo-Kazooie and Goldneye 007 on the NIntendo 64. Awkward controls aside, everything ran alright. Nintendo 64 performance could probably be a bit better, admittedly, but it's definitely playable.

There are some caveats, though

It's not all perfect

I set things up the best I could so that the experience was as console-like as possible. I disabled the PIN on my phone, so I can wake it up and unlock it using the controller. I also tried to set ES-DE as my default home app, but this is where I ran into the first major problem with this setup.

When ES-DE is set as the home screen app on this phone, it starts loading in a vertical orientation, and it's simply not something I can fix. It always works this way, and even using the "rotate screen" feature in ES-DE itself doesn't work. The UI rotates on my phone's screen, but my TV still receives a vertical signal, so it just doesn't work. Instead, I ended up keeping Niagara Launcher as my home screen app. Surprisingly, it works great with a controller, and while the vertical layout doesn't make sense for a TV, it means that I can launch ES-DE and have it rotate properly so it works way better.

Even then, things aren't perfect. This phone doesn't let me use an external screen on its own, so it just mirrors the built-in display. This uses more power and wears down the OLED panel, but I minimized the damage by setting the phone's screen to the absolute minimum brightness. That didn't do much to fix the aspect ratio, though. TVs are 16:9, but phones like this have taller aspect ratios, so even with the proper orientation, there's some letterboxing on my TV screen. It's not a huge problem, but certainly not ideal.

This controller turned my smartphone into the ultimate Game Boy

If you're looking for a cheap controller to play retro games on your phone, it doesn't get better than GameSir's Pocket Taco.

5
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Otherwise, I have to say I actually hate Bluetooth, and getting my Xbox controller to reliably pair with this phone meant painstakingly unpairing it from every other device in the house, and even disabling Bluetooth on my main device. Eventually, I did get it to work, but if you have the money to invest, I'd also consider looking for a controller that uses a proprietary wireless dongle. Since you're using a USB hub, you may have the extra USB port anyway, and the connection could be way more reliable.

A great use for an old phone

Even with all my complaints at the end there, make no mistake, I think this was a fun and worthwhile project. It's a great way to repurpose an old phone and a great way to enjoy retro games without adding a loud fan to the living or skyrocketing your electricity bill. And because it's a small device, it's also easy to fit next to your TV without taking up too much space.

item.title: These 6 Android Auto habits are quietly ruining your driving experience
item.itunes:title: These 6 Android Auto habits are quietly ruining your driving experience
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Android Auto remains one of the best infotainment platforms for your car, replacing your built-in system with Google's mirroring ecosystem. If you're a regular Android Auto user, you probably have your desired settings and apps configured on your phone. That said, you may have missed some of the app's less obvious features.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Everyone has their Android Auto habits, but yours might be holding back your experience on every drive. The good news is that changing these habits isn't hard; you just need to set up a few things (just once) to get the most out of Android Auto. From using a wired connection on long drives and setting up split-screen to saving a handful of pinned commands, you could improve your driving experience considerably.

Not downloading offline maps before a trip

Mobile data might betray you

We would all love universal connectivity on our drives, but that's rarely how it goes. The moment you leave your city, even on a slightly longer drive, there are bound to be areas with spotty signal. Losing connectivity when you're unprepared can be frustrating, as it can cut off navigation, music playback, and voice commands.

This is where an age-old trick comes in: downloading offline maps. Before you leave for your destination, download an offline copy of the entire route in Google Maps. If you frequent the same locations a few times a year, you could save the corresponding map data permanently. This keeps your navigation going even if you don't have your favorite tunes to hum to — Poweramp can handle that even without a premium streaming subscription.

While Google Maps can work offline, there are better options, such as Organic Maps, which is powered by a community-driven offline maps experience. You don't need to download any navigation data in advance, which makes it more convenient.

4 lesser-known Android Auto apps that solve problems Google Maps and Spotify pretend don't exist

These apps actually handle edge cases well.

5
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Ignoring background activity and network switching settings

Android Auto needs to be one of the exceptions

Android Auto runs on your phone, which means it's subject to the same network and battery restrictions Android loves to implement for every other app. Well, that's unless you toggle a few settings beforehand. Android's intelligent network switching can disrupt the connection with your car as your phone tries to switch to better Wi-Fi. To stop this behavior, disable Switch to better Wi-Fi networks in your Wi-Fi settings.

The other setting you should disable is background restrictions on Android Auto. Your phone automatically suspends some apps when they're in the background, but you don't want this to happen with Android Auto. It relies on background activity to keep navigation and media playback running without interruptions. You can add Android Auto to your list of unrestricted apps or find its battery usage settings and select Unrestricted after enabling background usage.

Not using automatic startup

You're missing out on one of the best features

If you rely on wireless Android Auto more than wired mode, enable automatic startup if you haven't already. If you're still manually connecting Android Auto to your car every time you drive, you're not getting the full Android Auto experience. Toggling automatic startup connects as soon as you open the car door.

To enable this, turn Start Android Auto automatically on under Connected devices or the connectivity settings on your phone. You can also turn on Start Android Auto while locked and Start music automatically for a truly hands-off start to your drive.

Sticking to wireless even on long drives

Convenience over reliability doesn't always work

Android Auto is more convenient when you don't have your phone chained to the screen permanently. However, it remains the easier option only as long as it doesn't start acting up. Failure to connect to the car or frequent disconnections are still common problems with Android Auto. Longer drives make these problems more likely, so it's best to trust a wired connection when you want reliability.

Android Auto won't connect to the car automatically, but it's a small price to pay for a satisfying long-drive experience. Wireless beats wired during short drives, but it isn't as universally convenient as some drivers might believe. Keep a high-quality USB data-and-charging cable, preferably under 3 feet in length, in your car at all times.

Relying on voice commands for everything

There's a limit to Gemini's intelligence

With Gemini replacing Google Assistant in Android Auto, most people are probably relying more and more on voice commands. Controlling navigation, media playback, calls, and messages is definitely more convenient than fiddling with the screen when driving, but you can at least configure automations for some frequently used actions.

Gemini Actions allows you to customize your Android Auto launcher by adding pinned actions. So, whenever you get into your car, you can simply tap a saved action on the launcher that sets your navigation to your office, checks your first calendar event, and starts your favorite playlist, all at once. This not only automates repetitive tasks but can also execute other actions when background noise interferes with Gemini voice commands.

For instance, you could set up pinned actions to "Tell me the remaining items on my Google Tasks grocery list" or "Find the nearest rest stop." When you want to run these tasks without speaking a long voice command amid noise, these pinned actions can come in handy.

Using the default screen layout

You can choose your preference

If you have a decently large screen, Android Auto's split-screen layout becomes one of its most impressive features. Most people only need two things on the screen during most drives: maps and music. With the split-screen layout, you don't need to constantly switch between Maps and YouTube Music—they're both on the screen at the same time. However, most users don't know that they can tweak the default layout.

You can choose between Media Closer to Driver and Navigation Closer to Driver in Android Auto's Advanced settings. While you should always keep your eyes on the road, having your preferred app closer helps when you need to act quickly. Choosing your preferred layout makes this awfully simple.

I changed one Android Auto setting, and I don't miss the bottom taskbar at all now

Toggling Quick Controls no longer moves the taskbar with every vehicle.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

The default Android Auto experience isn't the best

Many drivers never think to tweak the default settings on Android Auto, sticking with whatever appears on the screen. Often, the best features are hidden in settings you probably never touched. If you want Android Auto to work for you, tune it to your preferences. None of the changes above take too long, and the payoff is incredible.

item.title: My Wi-Fi 7 mesh was stuck at gigabit speeds, and the problem was one port I forgot about
item.itunes:title: My Wi-Fi 7 mesh was stuck at gigabit speeds, and the problem was one port I forgot about
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Picking up a Wi-Fi 7 mesh system doesn't automatically raise real-world client throughput past 1 Gbps. Your entire data path needs to be compatible with your new Wi-Fi 7 router. If there's an issue, even down to a single 1 GbE link somewhere between your router, satellite node, switch, or local storage target, this can stop your data from achieving the speeds that you were promised from the hardware. If you've recently deployed a Wi-Fi 7 router, and you're finding that your speeds just aren't where you were expecting them to be, it might be worth isolating the bottleneck via LAN testing and double-checking if a single port is throttling your speeds.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
Wi-Fi 7 will not fix what's actually wrong with your home network

A new router alone won't upgrade your network to Wi-Fi 7

1
By  Tanveer Singh

Wi-Fi 7 doesn't always deliver

There are many factors that contribute to speeds

Wi-Fi 7, otherwise referred to as the IEEE 802.11be standard, introduces features such as up to 320 MHz channel bandwidth in the 6 GHz band, 4096-QAM modulation (12 bits per symbol versus 10 bits in 1024-QAM), and multi-link operation typically across 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands (with peak theoretical PHY rates cited up to 46 Gbps across the standard's maximum configuration). In practice consumer clients will rarely reach theoretical PHY ceilings due to protocol overhead, spatial stream counts, distance, interference, and congestion but the fact that that's physically possible is outstanding.

When I deployed my Wi-Fi 7 hardware, I found that I was capping out at less than 950 Mbps despite what the hardware is actually capable of. This was because many multi-gigabit Wi-Fi 7 routers and mesh nodes, mine included, ship with a mix of 2.5 GbE or 10 GbE ports alongside one or more legacy 1 GbE ports for LAN, WAN, or secondary backup/uplink roles. I used this single 1 GbE link and it meant that my speeds were capped at 1000 Mbps. In the real world a TCP payload throughput typically tops out near 930 to 950 Mbps after Ethernet, IP, and TCP header overhead.

Because I overlooked that port, it in turn throttled my entire path. Even if a client associates over Wi-Fi 7 at multi-gigabit link rates near a node, traffic destined for or routed through an upstream gateway, downstream switch, or local server traverses every hop in series. If one forgotten port negotiates at 1 Gbps rather than 2.5 GBASE-T or 10 GBASE-T, that link becomes the choke point for any flow crossing it.
